title: Yoghurt with Honey and Walnuts
subtitle: Greek yoghurt drizzled with honey and scattered with walnuts, the Greek way
excerpt: Greek yoghurt with honey and walnuts is one of the oldest breakfasts still eaten daily, and one of the few recipes where the quality of each individual ingredient is the entire point. Thick sheep's milk yoghurt, dark thyme honey, and bitter walnuts. Three things, properly chosen, needing nothing else.
sourceNotes: Yoghurt with honey and walnuts, yiaourti me meli kai karidia, is a traditional Greek breakfast and dessert eaten across Greece and Cyprus. The combination of strained yoghurt (traditionally from sheep's or goat's milk), thyme honey from the mountains of Crete or Hymettus near Athens, and walnuts has been part of Greek food culture for centuries.

content.text: Yoghurt with honey and walnuts is a lesson in ingredient quality over technique. There is no cooking, no method to master. The three components either work together or they don't, depending entirely on what you use. Use {{greek-yoghurt}} Greek yoghurt that is thick enough to hold a spoon upright. Use {{honey}} honey with genuine character rather than pale supermarket blends. Break {{walnuts}} walnuts into rough pieces by hand rather than buying them pre-chopped, which taste noticeably staler. A pinch of cinnamon is optional but traditional in parts of Greece and adds warmth against the tang of the yoghurt.

items.prepNote: runny; thyme honey if you can find it

content.text: Spoon the {{greek-yoghurt}} Greek yoghurt into two bowls or onto two plates. If the yoghurt has separated slightly in the pot, stir it briefly first. Roughly break the {{walnuts}} walnuts on the chopping board, a few quick chops with the knife is enough; you want irregular pieces, not dust. Drizzle the {{honey}} honey over the yoghurt and scatter the walnuts over the top. If you're using cinnamon, dust it over last. Eat immediately.

In Greece, this appears at the breakfast table and as a dessert with equal frequency. The honey that matters most is thyme honey, dark, intensely aromatic, with a slight herbal bitterness that cuts through the fat of the yoghurt in a way that lighter honeys can't. It comes primarily from Crete, where wild thyme grows across the hillsides, and from the slopes of Hymettus near Athens, where it has been prized since antiquity. Plato wrote about Hymettus honey; Ovid mentioned it in his poetry. If you can get Greek thyme honey from a deli or specialist food shop, the dish is transformed. Acacia honey or any clear runny honey will also work and is worth using over a thick, cheap blend. The yoghurt in Greece is traditionally from sheep's milk, much richer and tangier than cow's milk versions. Full-fat cow's milk Greek yoghurt is a perfectly good substitute and the kind you'll find in most UK supermarkets.
Add a few fresh figs when they're in season, halved or quartered, placed alongside the walnuts.
A small handful of pomegranate seeds instead of or alongside the walnuts adds colour and a sharp contrast.
Serve on a flat plate rather than a bowl for a more elegant presentation, the honey pools attractively and the walnuts sit better.
